insider_note: Three types, with an example for the first two: malonic acid against succinate for competitive, copper and mercury ions for non-competitive. Feedback inhibition is answered by its definition, not by an example.

steps.label: What an inhibitor is
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the three names. Number them so the next three steps can follow.
lines: Enzyme inhibitors are chemicals that STOP or
slow the activity of an enzyme.
The process is called inhibition.
There are three types:
1. Competitive  2. Non-competitive
3. Feedback
steps.why: Listing the three types before explaining them shows the shape of the answer. The first two are named by WHERE the inhibitor binds; the third is named by WHAT does the inhibiting.
common_mistakes: Saying inhibitors destroy the enzyme. They stop its ACTIVITY; most do not destroy it.
Naming only two types. The guide gives three, and each is a mark.
steps.memory_tip: Two are named by where the inhibitor binds: the active site, or another site. The third is named by what inhibits: the end product.

steps.label: Competitive inhibitors
steps.margin_note: Resemblance, active site, example. All three parts of the mark.
lines: 1. COMPETITIVE INHIBITORS:
These resemble the substrate in shape.
They bind to the ACTIVE SITE and so compete
with the substrate.
Example: malonic acid resembles the substrate
succinate and inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
steps.why: The inhibitor works only because it looks like the substrate, so the resemblance is the definition rather than an extra detail.
common_mistakes: Saying a competitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. It binds AT the active site.
Leaving out the resemblance to the substrate. That is what makes it competitive.
steps.memory_tip: It looks like the substrate, so it takes the substrate's seat.

steps.label: Non-competitive inhibitors
steps.margin_note: No resemblance, a different site, the shape change, an example.
lines: 2. NON-COMPETITIVE INHIBITORS:
These have NO structural similarity to the
substrate.
They bind at a site OTHER than the active site.
This changes the globular shape of the enzyme,
so it can no longer work.
Example: metal ions of copper and mercury.
steps.why: Changing the enzyme's shape from somewhere else disables the active site indirectly, which is why adding more substrate cannot overcome this kind of inhibitor.
common_mistakes: Saying it resembles the substrate. It does NOT — that is the competitive kind.
Leaving out the shape change. Changing the globular structure is how it works.
steps.memory_tip: It does not take the seat; it bends the chair.

steps.label: Feedback inhibitors
steps.margin_note: Definition, the words 'end product', and one line on why the cell does it.

lines.text: The end product switches its own pathway off

lines: 3. FEEDBACK INHIBITION:
A cellular control mechanism in which the
enzyme's own END PRODUCT inhibits its activity.
It is part of the homeostatic control of
metabolism.
It stops the cell making more of a product it
already has enough of.
steps.why: The product itself is the signal, so the cell needs no separate sensor to know when to stop.
common_mistakes: Saying the substrate inhibits the enzyme. It is the END PRODUCT.
Leaving out the purpose. Feedback inhibition prevents wasteful overproduction.
steps.memory_tip: Enough product means stop making product.
